title: DBLab vs Tiger Data: clones of any Postgres vs Tiger Cloud forks
description: Tiger Data forks a Tiger Cloud service, now or from a past point, with copy-on-write on free services. DBLab clones any PostgreSQL on a machine you control.
summary: Tiger Data, formerly Timescale, runs Tiger Cloud, a hosted PostgreSQL service with TimescaleDB. A fork is an independent copy of a Tiger Cloud service, from now, the last daily backup or a past timestamp. Free services fork in about 30 to 90 seconds on copy-on-write storage; standard services restore from backup and WAL, typically in 5 to 20+ minutes. DBLab Engine is open-source software that makes full-size thin clones of any PostgreSQL, wherever it runs, on a machine you control. If production runs on Tiger Cloud, its forks are the direct path. If production stays elsewhere, DBLab clones it in place.
chooseThem: Your database already runs on Tiger Cloud. A fork is made from the service itself in the Console, with the tiger CLI or through MCP, with no second copy to load and no clone server to run.
Forks from a past state: from the last daily backup or any timestamp within the recovery period, 3 days on Performance and 14 days on Scale.
Free services use copy-on-write storage: a fork takes about 30 to 90 seconds, and only chunks that diverge from the parent are billed.
A ready-made GitHub Action, timescale/fork-service, forks a service when a pull request opens, runs the tests against the fork and cleans up.
Tiger MCP is built into the open-source Tiger CLI, with a service_fork tool and a read-only mode that turns off mutating tools.

rows.them: Tiger Cloud is a hosted PostgreSQL platform with the TimescaleDB extension. A fork is an exact copy of a Tiger Cloud service at a point in time, with its own data, configuration and compute, used for testing, analysis and recovery.

Forks are made from Tiger Cloud services. Other PostgreSQL databases, including Amazon RDS and Aurora, get there by migration: Livesync replication keeps the target in sync until cutover, or pg_dump for databases under 100 GB where downtime is acceptable.

Free services use copy-on-write storage (Fluid Storage) with zero-copy between a fork and the parent. Standard services use traditional storage with backup restore plus WAL. By default a fork gets compute that matches the parent's resources.
Free services: about 30 to 90 seconds. Standard services: varies with the size of the service, typically 5 to 20+ minutes.

A fork contains the database data and schema, the configuration and an admin user with a new password. Strategies: now, the last snapshot (backups are daily), or a timestamp within the plan's recovery period.
Not documented in the sources we reviewed.

The GitHub Action timescale/fork-service forks a service when a pull request is opened, from now or the last snapshot, runs tests and migrations against the fork, then cleans it up. It authenticates with a Tiger Cloud API key.

Tiger Console, the tiger CLI (tiger service fork) and Tiger MCP, built into the CLI, with a service_fork tool. Read-only mode turns off mutating tools, fork included. The CLI installs the MCP server for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, VS Code and others.
Tiger Cloud forks run in Tiger Data's hosted service, on AWS or Azure. TimescaleDB Enterprise, in public beta, runs on your own Linux servers, and its console can fork a service there.

TimescaleDB is on GitHub; its LICENSE file puts code outside the tsl directory under Apache 2.0 and code inside it under the Timescale License. The Tiger CLI is under Apache 2.0. Forks are part of the hosted Tiger Cloud service.

Point-in-time recovery and forking: 3 days on Performance, 14 days on Scale; the docs list up to 180 days on Enterprise. A service cannot be forked while it is provisioning or changing state. Free services, the copy-on-write ones, are in beta; two are included on all plans.

A fork is a service of its own: compute metered hourly, storage by average GB per hour. On copy-on-write storage only chunks that diverge from the parent are billed; on traditional storage the whole fork is. Tiered chunks are billed once, however many forks exist.

pricing.notes: Hourly billing; storage $0.177/GB-month, an effective price that assumes 5x compression; up to 4 services; point-in-time recovery 3 days; 30-day free trial
Hourly billing; storage $0.212/GB-month, an effective price that assumes 5x compression; unlimited services; point-in-time recovery 14 days

pricingNote: Tiger Cloud charges by consumption: compute is metered hourly and storage by average GB per hour.

faq.q: Can Tiger Data fork a database that runs on Amazon RDS?
faq.a: Not in place. Tiger Cloud forks are made from Tiger Cloud services, so the data has to be migrated first, for example with Livesync replication, which works with RDS and Aurora when logical replication is enabled. DBLab clones such databases where they are, by dump and restore.

faq.q: How long does a Tiger Cloud fork take?
faq.a: About 30 to 90 seconds for free services, which use copy-on-write storage. Standard services restore from backup plus WAL and typically take 5 to 20+ minutes, depending on size.

faq.q: Is Tiger Data the same company as Timescale?
faq.a: Yes. Timescale changed its name to Tiger Data on June 17, 2025. The cloud service is called Tiger Cloud, and the open-source extension remains TimescaleDB.

faq.q: What is Ghost from Tiger Data?
faq.a: Ghost is hosted Postgres you spin up, fork and throw away, made by Tiger Data. Its site says Ghost is winding down: it no longer accepts new users and will be shut down eventually, with a timeline and export instructions to follow.

faq.q: Does Tiger Data have an MCP server for agents?
faq.a: Yes. Tiger MCP ships inside the open-source Tiger CLI. Its service_fork tool forks a service into an independent copy, and read-only mode can turn off mutating tools or block them on services tagged PROD.

proofs.them: A Tiger Cloud fork of a standard service is a backup restore plus WAL replay and typically takes 5 to 20+ minutes, depending on size. Free services, in beta, fork in about 30 to 90 seconds on copy-on-write storage.
Tiger Cloud forks are made from Tiger Cloud services. A database on Amazon RDS, Aurora or another PostgreSQL is migrated first, with Livesync replication or pg_dump.

A Tiger Cloud fork is a service of its own, with compute billed by the hour. A fork of a standard service on traditional storage is billed for the storage of the whole service; only tiered chunks are shared.
Tiger Cloud forks run in Tiger Data's hosted service. TimescaleDB Enterprise runs on your own Linux servers and can fork a service there; it is in public beta.
